profile.name: Kaze no bon
profile.tagline: A 300-year-old night festival in Yatsuo where unmarried dancers hide their faces from typhoons.
profile.insight: In Yatsuo's steep lantern-lit streets, young unmarried dancers conceal their faces beneath low-brimmed straw hats to appease wind gods during nightly processions.
profile.profile: Kaze no bon is a night festival held annually from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, Toyama, Japan, dating back over 300 years to the Genroku era. Young unmarried men and women dance in long parallel lines through the village's steep, lantern-lit streets, their faces hidden by flat straw hats called amigasa. The dancers wear matching traditional attire—women in yukata and men in short jackets—and move slowly to the melancholic Etchu Owara Bushi music, featuring kokyū, shamisen, and taiko drums. Each dance troupe represents one of the district's eleven quarters, and the dances include the traditional Kyu odori and the Shin odori, introduced in 1920 with distinct male and female steps.
profile.profile_long:
Kaze no bon, also known as Owara Kaze no bon, is a traditional Japanese festival held every year from September 1 to 3 in the mountain village of Yatsuo, part of Toyama city on Honshū's western coast. The festival has been celebrated continuously since the Genroku era (1688-1704), originating as a ritual to appease typhoons and ensure a bountiful rice harvest during a season prone to storms. The event unfolds at night, transforming Yatsuo's narrow, steep, cobbled streets into a glowing corridor lined with paper lanterns. 

The festival's dancers are exclusively young unmarried men and women, reflecting a traditional belief that their virginal status protects them from divine wrath, though modern interpretations suggest the dance also serves social functions. The dancers wear traditional attire: women don cotton yukata and flat straw hats called amigasa, which are tilted low to conceal their faces, while men wear short jackets and similar hats. This concealment is meant to shield them from the anger of the wind gods they seek to pacify.

Dancers move slowly in long parallel lines representing the eleven quarters of the district, creating a solemn yet mesmerizing procession. The choreography includes two main dances: the Kyu odori, the older traditional dance, and the Shin odori, introduced in 1920, where men's steps mimic agricultural labor, differing from the women's movements. The dance steps are deliberate and restrained, emphasizing grace and subtlety over vigorous motion.

The musical accompaniment is central to the festival's atmosphere. At the procession's rear, musicians—typically older men and women—perform the Etchu Owara Bushi, a traditional local song. The ensemble features the kokyū, a rare bowed lute, the shamisen, a three-stringed plucked instrument, and taiko drums. A distinctive, well-aged female voice leads the singing, lending a melancholic tone to the music. This soundscape is recognized as one of Japan's 100 Soundscapes of Japan, selected by the Ministry of the Environment in 1996.

Beyond the dances and music, the festival includes traditional games, food stalls, and shops selling local crafts such as special Japanese paper, which visitors often take as souvenirs. Performances also occur on small stages throughout the village, and private shows take place in restaurants and homes. After tourists depart late at night, locals continue dancing in costume, sometimes until dawn.

Kaze no bon remains a living tradition, attracting up to 200,000 visitors annually, drawn by its unique blend of ritual, artistry, and the haunting beauty of its nighttime setting. The festival embodies a deep connection between community, nature, and spirituality, expressed through its distinctive dances, music, and the symbolic concealment of the dancers' faces.

sections.origins_and_history: Kaze no bon has been held without interruption since the Genroku era (1688-1704) in Yatsuo, Toyama, Japan. It originated as a festival to honor Shinto deities and to protect rice crops from typhoons common in early September. The tradition of dancers hiding their faces beneath low-brimmed straw hats stems from a belief that the gods' wrath might fall on them if seen. The festival has evolved into a popular tourist event while maintaining its original ritualistic purpose.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed at night in Yatsuo's steep, lantern-lit streets. Young unmarried men and women dance in long parallel lines, each line representing one of the eleven district quarters. Women wear yukata and flat straw hats (amigasa) tilted low to cover their faces; men wear short jackets and similar hats. There are two main dances: Kyu odori (traditional) and Shin odori (introduced in 1920), with distinct male and female steps. Men's steps evoke fieldwork. The movements are slow and deliberate, emphasizing grace and subtlety. Technique details beyond formation and basic costume are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music, known as Etchu Owara Bushi, is performed by older musicians at the rear of the procession. It features a melancholic, well-aged female vocal lead, accompanied by the kokyū (a rare bowed lute), shamisen (three-stringed plucked instrument), and taiko drums. This ensemble creates a haunting and nostalgic sound unique to the region. The music is recognized as one of Japan's 100 Soundscapes by the Ministry of the Environment.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional attire: women in cotton yukata and men in short jackets. Both wear flat straw hats called amigasa, tilted low to conceal their faces as a sign of respect and protection from the gods. The festival takes place at night in Yatsuo's narrow, steep, cobbled streets, illuminated by rows of paper lanterns, creating a mystical atmosphere.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Held annually from September 1 to 3, the festival honors Shinto deities to protect against typhoons and ensure a good rice harvest. The concealment of dancers' faces symbolizes appeasement of the wind gods. The event also serves social functions, allowing young unmarried people to meet. It includes public processions, stage performances, private shows, and local festivities with food and crafts.
sections.lineage: Kaze no bon is a form of Bon Odori, a category of Japanese folk dances performed during the Bon festival season. It is specific to Yatsuo in Toyama Prefecture and has maintained its unique musical and choreographic identity since the Genroku era.

claims.text: Kaze-no-Bon is a Japanese festival held every year from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, Toyama, Japan.
claims.quote: Kaze-no-Bon (風の盆) is a Japanese festival held every year from September 1 to 3 in Yatsuo, Toyama, Japan.

claims.text: The festival has a history of about 300 years, originating in the Genroku era (1688-1704).
claims.quote: Le festival existe sans interruption depuis l'ère Genroku (1688-1704), soit depuis plus de trois cents ans.

claims.text: Young unmarried men and women dance in long parallel lines, their faces covered by low-brimmed straw hats called amigasa.
claims.quote: Jeunes hommes et jeunes femmes, tous célibataires, progressent lentement en longues files parallèles... Les danseuses sont vêtues de yukata... et de chapeaux de paille plats dits amigasa, inclinés pour couvrir leur visage.

claims.text: The music features the kokyū, shamisen, and taiko drums, with a well-aged female vocal lead.
claims.quote: This particular style of music... using the somewhat-unknown kokyū... A well-aged female voice and a traditional shamisen often accompanies the kokyū.

claims.text: The dances include Kyu odori (traditional) and Shin odori (introduced in 1920), with men's steps evoking fieldwork.
claims.quote: La plus traditionnelle des danses est le Kyu odori; l'autre est le Shin odori, introduite en 1920 : dans celle-ci, les pas des hommes et des femmes différent, ceux des premiers évoquant les travaux des champs.

claims.text: The festival takes place at night in Yatsuo's steep, lantern-lit streets, creating a unique atmosphere.
claims.quote: The festival is uniquely held at night... The streets are decorated with paper lanterns.
